title: Ang 366–369: Guru Ram Das in Asa
tomorrow: how can a plan falling apart ever taste sweet?
last: KABIR'S ALPHABET · THE CITY WITHOUT SORROW.

cards: Every wedding has a moment everyone waits for: the vows, the ring, the first dance. At a Sikh wedding, it's four rounds. The couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib while four hymns are sung, one for each round.
Those hymns, the Lavan, are Guru Ram Das's, the fourth Guru's. They sit in another raga, Suhi. But his voice reaches Asa first, on ang 366.

teach.b: His hymns in Asa run from ang 366 to 369, headed Mahala 4, the fourth.
They're short, and they keep coming back to two things: longing for the Beloved, and the sangat, the company of the Guru's people, where the Name is sung together.
The voice that wrote the wedding rounds writes here like someone in love, waiting at a door with friends.
That's worth knowing before a wedding: the four rounds aren't a private moment staged for an audience.
The couple walks them inside the singing of everyone in the room, the sangat carrying them round. And the same company is there in Asa, on an ordinary morning, with no wedding at all.
Which ties up the whole week. Kabir's letters point at what they can't hold. Ravidas dreams a city with no gate.
So Dar asks what that door is like.
Guru Nanak looks for the light, then names the harm. Guru Amar Das lets the ego go into the ground. And Guru Ram Das sings at the door, in good company.

how: At an Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding, the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib four times as Guru Ram Das's four Lavan are read and sung; his Asa hymns, headed Mahala 4, are read in order after Guru Amar Das's.

practice: Read one short hymn on ang 366 if you can. Then count, slowly, on your fingers, the people whose company keeps you steady: one finger, one name. When you run out of fingers or names, rest with the ones you counted.
